intro: Four modules cover the whole job: how a help desk works, a troubleshooting method you can reuse, how to talk to people, and how to handle everyday issues safely. Practice in the labs: log and prioritise a ticket, diagnose a PC, and work through customer scenarios.

modules.title: How a help desk works
modules.summary: Understand tickets, incidents and requests, support tiers, priority and SLAs, escalation, and the knowledge base.

guide.html: The help desk is the single point of contact where people ask for IT help. It records every contact, fixes what it can, routes the rest to the right specialists, and keeps the customer informed. Good support is measured by how quickly and how well problems are solved, and by whether the same problem comes back.

Everything is recorded in a ticket so nothing is forgotten and work can be handed over. Common types:

  • Incident: something that was working is broken or degraded ("I can't print").
  • Service request: a standard thing the user is entitled to ask for ("I need access to the shared drive", a new laptop).
  • Problem: the underlying cause behind repeated incidents (every Monday the VPN drops). A problem record lets the team fix the root cause once.
  • Change: a planned modification, such as a patch or new software, approved and scheduled to reduce risk.

A good ticket contains who, what, when, where, the exact error message, what has been tried, and the impact.

• Self-service / Tier 0: password reset portals and knowledge base articles.
  • Tier 1: first contact. Logs the ticket, gathers details, fixes common issues, and escalates.
  • Tier 2: deeper technical skills, such as desktop, server or network specialists.
  • Tier 3: experts, engineers and vendors for the hardest problems.

Functional escalation passes the ticket to a team with more skill. Hierarchical escalation informs management because an issue is high-impact or the SLA is at risk. Escalate with everything you learned so the next person does not start over.

Priority comes from two questions: impact (how many people or how much business is affected) and urgency (how soon it must be fixed). A server outage that stops the whole company is high impact and high urgency (P1). One user's broken mouse is low impact and low urgency (P4). The loudest caller does not decide priority; the business impact does.

A service level agreement (SLA) sets targets for how fast you must respond and resolve by priority, for example P1 response in 15 minutes and resolution in 4 hours. Watch the clock and escalate before a target is missed.

A knowledge base (KB) stores tested fixes as short articles, so the next technician (or the user, through self-service) solves the issue faster. When you solve something new, write it up. Teams track first contact resolution, time to resolve, SLA compliance, ticket volume by category and customer satisfaction to find recurring problems and improve.

tips: Impact times urgency decides priority, not who shouts loudest.
Record everything in the ticket, even quick fixes.
Escalate with full notes so the next tier does not repeat your questions.
Watch the SLA clock; escalate before a target is missed.
If you solve something new, add it to the knowledge base.
terms: Ticket
A record of a request or problem, from opening to closing.
Incident
An unplanned interruption or reduction in quality of a service.
Service request
A standard request, such as new access or equipment.
Problem
The root cause behind one or more incidents.
SLA
Service level agreement: agreed response and resolution times.
Escalation
Handing a ticket to a more skilled team or to management.
First contact resolution
Solving the issue on the first call or chat.
Knowledge base
A library of documented fixes and how-tos.

modules.title: A troubleshooting method
modules.summary: Follow a repeatable process: gather facts, form a theory, test it, fix, verify, and document. Ask good questions and change one thing at a time.

guide.html: Guessing and clicking at random wastes time and can make things worse. A method keeps you calm, gets to the cause faster, and gives you notes to hand over. The widely used outline is: identify the problem; establish a theory; test the theory; plan and implement; verify; document.

Gather information before touching anything. Good questions:

  • What exactly happens? What is the exact error message?
  • What were you trying to do, and when did it last work?
  • What changed recently (updates, new software, moved desks, password change)?
  • Is anyone else affected? Does it happen on another device or network?
  • Can you show me or send a screenshot?

Then try to reproduce it and back up important data before making changes. Confirm the real problem: users often describe a symptom ("the internet is down") rather than the cause.

List probable causes, starting with the simple and obvious: power, cables, wrong network, Caps Lock, an unplugged adapter. Then work from what is most likely and cheapest to check.

Test each theory with a quick, safe check (ping, swap a cable, try another account). If the theory is wrong, form a new one. If you run out of ideas or lack access or skill, escalate. Useful techniques: divide and conquer (is it the device, the network, or the service?), compare with a working machine, and change only one thing at a time so you know what fixed it.

Plan the fix and consider side effects: do you need approval, a maintenance window, a backup, or a way to roll back? Then implement it. Verify that the original problem is gone, that the user agrees, and that nothing else broke; add preventive steps where you can (updates, a KB article, a monitoring alert). Finally document the symptoms, cause, steps and outcome in the ticket.

Many problems are easiest to find by working through layers. For "I can't reach the website": is the device powered and connected (physical)? Does it have an IP address (ipconfig)? Can it reach the gateway and the internet by IP (ping 8.8.8.8)? Can it resolve names (nslookup)? Does the site itself work for others? Each answer narrows the search by half.

tips: Ask for the exact error message or a screenshot.
Always ask: what changed recently?
Check the simple things first.
Change one thing at a time.
Verify with the user before closing the ticket.
Document even when it was quick.
terms: Theory of probable cause
Your best explanation of the problem, before you test it.
Reproduce
Make the problem happen again on purpose to study it.
Divide and conquer
Split the system in two and find which half has the fault.
Rollback plan
Steps to undo a change if it makes things worse.
Root cause
The underlying reason a problem happens.
Escalate
Hand the problem to someone with more skill or authority.

modules.title: Communication and customer service
modules.summary: Listen, set expectations, handle upset customers, explain in plain language, and write clear ticket notes.

guide.html: People contact the help desk when they are blocked, often stressed or in a hurry. Start by listening without interrupting. Let them finish, then repeat back what you understood: "So the printer shows an offline error since this morning, and you have a meeting at 2. Is that right?" That shows you care and catches misunderstandings early.

Avoid jargon. Say "your computer's connection to the network" instead of "your NIC's DHCP lease". Give one step at a time and check that the user has done it. Match the person's pace, stay patient, and never make anyone feel foolish: users are experts at their own jobs, not at IT. Use positive wording: "Here is what we can do" rather than "You can't". Never blame ("you should have...").

1. Stay calm and do not take it personally.
  2. Listen and let them vent briefly.
  3. Acknowledge the feeling: "I understand this is frustrating, especially with a deadline."
  4. Focus on the solution and what you will do now.
  5. Set expectations: what happens next and when, and then keep that promise.
  6. Follow up, or escalate if you cannot help.

Do not argue, make excuses, put the customer down, or promise something you cannot deliver.

Be honest about timing: "I will call you back by 3 pm with an update" is better than "soon". If you cannot fix it on the call, explain the next step, who owns it, and how the user will hear about it. When transferring or escalating, summarize the case to the next person so the customer does not repeat everything. Never leave a customer on hold without telling them why and checking back.

Notes are communication too. Write them so a stranger could continue the work: symptom (with the exact error), impact, steps tried and results, current status and next step. Keep it factual, professional and free of opinions or jokes about the customer. Remember that tickets may be read by the user, managers or auditors. Finally, treat what you see on screens and desks as confidential.

tips: Repeat back the problem to confirm you understand.
Acknowledge feelings before jumping to the fix.
Avoid jargon and blame.
Promise only what you can deliver, then deliver it.
Write ticket notes for a stranger.
Keep customer information confidential.
terms: Active listening
Giving full attention and confirming what you heard.
Empathy
Showing you understand how the person feels.
Expectation setting
Telling the customer what happens next and when.
Jargon
Technical words that confuse non-technical people.
Handoff
Passing a case to someone else with a clear summary.
Confidentiality
Not sharing or exposing private information.

modules.title: Everyday issues and safe support
modules.summary: Handle common requests quickly: passwords, network, printers, slow PCs and email, verify who you are helping, use remote tools safely, and recognise social engineering.

guide.html: Attackers often phone the help desk pretending to be an employee to get a password reset or MFA change. Before any account action, verify the person using your procedure: employee ID, a callback to the number on file, a manager's approval, or a verification code sent to a known device. Never ask for a user's password. Never reset an account on the strength of urgency or pressure alone ("I'm the CEO and I'm about to board"). Pressure is the red flag.

ReportQuick checks
Can't sign inCaps Lock, correct account and domain, locked or expired password, MFA device, then reset after verifying identity
No internet / networkWi-Fi or cable, ipconfig (169.254.x.x means no DHCP), ping the gateway, test DNS with nslookup, other devices affected?
Slow computerFree disk space, memory and CPU in Task Manager, startup programs, pending updates, malware scan, restart
Printer won't printPower and connection, offline status, queue stuck, correct printer selected, driver, paper and toner
Email problemsWebmail works? Network, full mailbox, wrong password, spam or rules, Outlook profile
Application crashesRestart, updates, repair or reinstall, exact error, recent changes

Remote tools (Remote Desktop, Quick Assist, vendor tools) let you fix things without visiting. Always get permission before connecting, tell the user what you are doing, use company-approved tools only, avoid viewing private data, and disconnect and log out when finished. Never use personal remote tools or leave unattended access running. Record the session in the ticket.

Help desk staff are targets. Watch for urgency, authority, unusual requests, requests to skip the process, and callers who know little but demand access. Teach users to report suspicious emails rather than delete them: hover over links, check the sender, never share codes or passwords. If a user clicked something, isolate the device, change passwords, and report to security straight away; speed matters.

Escalate when it needs access or skill you lack, affects many people, involves a security incident, risks data loss, or the SLA is about to be missed. A good escalation says what is wrong, the impact, what you tried, and what you need. Closing the loop matters too: tell the user what happened and confirm the fix before closing the ticket.

tips: Verify identity before any account change.
Never ask for or accept a password.
Urgency and pressure are social engineering red flags.
Get permission before connecting remotely, and log out afterward.
169.254.x.x means the PC could not get an address from DHCP.
Report phishing; do not just delete it.
terms: Social engineering
Tricking people into giving access or information.
Phishing
Fraudulent messages that steal credentials or install malware.
MFA
Multi-factor authentication: more than one proof of identity.
Remote support
Fixing a device over the network with the user's permission.
APIPA
169.254.x.x self-assigned address used when DHCP fails.
Least privilege
Giving only the access needed to do the job.

slides.title: Everyday issues and safe support
script: Most tickets are common problems. Solve them fast, and stay safe.

slides.title: Verify before you help
script: Always verify identity before resetting anything. Urgency and pressure are warning signs.

slides.title: Quick network checks
